utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Konings, I will remind you again that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony. I further would like to remind you and you as well, Mr. Kehoe, that we did not plan not to sit on Wednesday to give again an opportunity to interpreters and transcribers to recover. It was for other reasons. Would you please keep that in mind. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, when we left off last week, we were talking about the targets on P1271.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could bring that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Colonel, when you were asked some questions about this by Mr. Russo last week, and specifically talking about the first entry, the church in Knin, you noted on page 14432 at line 2 that: "The basic answer is a church should not be on a target list." When you were asked that question, Colonel, you were presuming that it was just a church and just a house of worship, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, because otherwise I would have -- I would have thought to have seen another target description.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go back to the mapping that we were engaged in on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That would be 1D65-0495.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And as we take these grid coordinates for the church in Knin, we can see from the chart that that is, in fact, the ARSK special police barracks, the St. Ante monastery. Now -- do you see that there, sir? You can see that --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Look towards the bottom centre, KV 110. That is the target.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And over on the left-hand side in the "A" box is the description that has been previously identified through evidence of this Court that identifies A5 as the St. Ante monastery, the ARSK special police headquarters.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, through the colours, it is hard for me it read what is in the red box especially.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Is it that any better, in the grey box down. It's A5, sir.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm trying to find it. Yes, I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now were you told that this was, in fact, a Catholic church?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall that if the officer of the Prosecutor told me that. But that in itself, that doesn't matter because whether it was a Catholic church, whether it's a mosque, that doesn't matter, because on the target list is a target which says church at Knin which says not that is a Special Forces headquarters. There is it no effect mentioned that you want to have against that target. So, to me, that is an utterly strange way of identifying targets. Because why not mentioning such an important target like special forces headquarters on the target list and mentioning the effect that you want to achieve there, because the Croatian army was using more or less the same types of effects that we use in NATO, so it is very easy if you want have that target either destroyed, neutralised, harassed, interdict, to mention the proper name of the target, the proper description, and not just -- well, leave it at church at Knin because is that something that will cause a lot of misunderstanding, will cause a lot of questioning afterward, and in a battle that may cause real trouble. I think it's very unwise to mention in the target list only church in Knin. I don't understand that. I don't understand when you want to attack a legal target, special forces headquarters, why mentioning -- because you may have another purpose. You may have another purpose. If I think very bad, you may have another purpose in indeed attacking that church. There is no proof of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, the important thing in getting this target is the grid coordinate, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The important thing in that is the grid coordinate. But last week we were discussing the other target, the hospital, and you mentioned that the hospital was -- was written wrong. Somebody had miswritten something. But in the same moment you can miswrite the grids. So actually when you say hospital or when you say church, you may mean church, and you may write down some other grids and have some agreement that the real target is hospital or church. That comes across my mind. And that is caused by the fact that you -- that in a target lists the names the description of the target is not properly done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But that would call upon the -- the people doing the shooting to check these grids, wouldn't it, and make sure that they're correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, that has to be done. But there can also be an understanding because that actually you mean the hospital, but for the purpose of a certain agreement, you write down grids that are in middle of a forest, and you know where the grids are, but you don't write them on a piece of paper. Because what I tried to say is that the target list that you show to me is a target list that mentions churches and hospitals, and although the grids are in another area, the fact of stating a church and a hospital and not mentioning the exact target that you want to achieve, I cannot understand, and I hope you can explain that to me, why in a military operation you mention on a target list the -- a church, a hospital, and not the proper targets that you want to attack because the proper targets, as you say, were known. The Croatian army wanted to attack the Special Forces police headquarters, and I don't discuss with you about that because I think that is a legal target.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, why would the Croatian want to shoot at a Catholic church?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not here to answer that question, but I do know that that kind of facts happens all through the Balkans, and that can be a part of the overall order that was given to the artillery shelling of the city of Knin because also there was no effect mentioned. Also there was no explanation given. So from my perspective - if I play devil's advocate - if I read in a target list church, hospital, and I see in the operational order for the artillery the order shelling the city of Knin --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't want to cut you off, Colonel, but the answer to the question is you don't know. I have a limited amount of time. The answer to the question is you don't know. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You don't know why the Croatian would shoot at their own Catholic church. You don't know.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I said that. No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't mean to cut you off, Colonel, but I do have a limited amount of time.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. I have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You were talking -- previously you were talking about correcting grids. Did you see evidence in the documents that was shown to you by the Prosecutor that the grids that we looked at at P1271 had been reviewed and had been corrected?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But that's not what I said before it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's my question, sir.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you -- go back to P1271. And I ask you to take a look at the X grid reference for the cross-roads, KV 510.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And is it -- in the initial documentation that the Prosecutor presented, it is 76130. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to Exhibit P1272, the third page of this document, and this is the artillery prep document introduced by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I go to page 3 of this document. And we can see an X grid reference for 510, the cross-roads as 7813. Now, let us go back to 1D65-0495. That should be -- the cross-roads is 78130; I apologise, it says 7813.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now we see the for KD 510, and it's difficult to see, but that would put it right in the middle of the UN base. Let us go to the next slide, please. And we see in the upper left-hand corner the initial grid coordinates in Exhibit P1271 which is 76130 described as the cross-roads, and we look at the new coordinates that are -- or the changes grid coordinates that are on P1272, and we have put that in KV 510, which is -- I'm sure you know upon reviewing the map in Knin, is, in fact, the cross-roads. This would reflect to you, would it not, Colonel, that the HV went through the care of taking these grid references and checking these grid references for accuracy prior to the attack, would it not?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's your conclusion. What I'm a bit puzzled because what I do have now is two documents, two different documents, which use two different coordinates, two different X grids, for the same target. Well, somebody corrected something, but I don't know what is the real KV 510. What was used in the actual attack on Knin. I don't have that information. I only have two sets of different grids with the same target number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, as on the map you have before you, you have reviewed Knin and been in Knin, as we look at KV 510 as it's corrected with the green arrow, that is it, in fact, the cross-roads in Knin, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the cross-roads in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go to the next map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, the grid references for the cross-roads were checked and changed. Yet the grid references for the title hospital were not changed. And I'm sure that you know that the target KV 710 was, in fact, this in field adjacent to the ARSK unit in the high school. So we can assume, can we not, sir, or you can conclude that someone went through these lists, corrected them, didn't correct the one targeted hospital because they wanted to fire on this field adjacent to this hospital where there was, in fact, a mortar unit observed?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Kehoe is putting a hypothetical that this -- where the KV 10 target is indicated on this map is actually are where the mortar section was located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that as a matter of fact it's on the basis of the questions and the evidence led by Mr. Kehoe that he intended to say that a mortar unit was served nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Nearby.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you answer that, sir, or do you want to ask it again?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sure, absolutely. So we can assume, can we not, sir, or you could conclude that someone went through these lists and corrected them and didn't correct the one targeted hospital because they wanted to fire on this field that was near to the area where a mortar unit was observed. Can you not conclude that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's just one conclusion. I have another conclusion for you as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'd like to offer 1D65-0495 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D1271, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1271 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Talking again about this St. Ante's monastery which is discussed as number 6 in your list of targets in your addendum, you were told to assume that the St. Ante's monastery was headquarters for the ARSK special police. Were you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On page 5 of your hypothetical facts, I believe you were given a fact on number five. "ARSK police" -- special police headquarters, and I'm reading from your Annex A to your addendum. Do you have that, sir. Do you have a hard copy?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any hard copy here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, with the assistance of the usher. Thank you, Mr. Misetic. This is P1260, and this -- is it as Annex A which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be find in the binder, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: It was in tab 4 of the binder of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I know this is it a lot of information, Colonel, and there is a lot going on, so please take your time referring back to these reports. We read at number of your --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That the ARSK special police headquarters was the St. Ante monastery, right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the -- you also note that in here that the police were attached to the military. Right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you told that there was police -- had also been deployed to the front lines?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you -- what you told me last week, and that was what I was reading in the information on the -- on the enemy, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With regard to this headquarters, were you told that after Operation Storm, 20 cases of ammunition was found at this -- this headquarters, this ARSK special police headquarters at St. Ante monastery. And I'm referring to D57 for the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, page 15853, entry 43 out of 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you told that, sir?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have been given the information that we have in front of me which, by the way, also says also housed Serb civilian refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We'll get to that, sir, because I want to talk to you a little bit about that issue. But you realised when you were reviewing this that the HV was not, in fact, targeting a church but was targeting a headquarters for a special police, an ARSK special police, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll put aside some of the other issues, but given the fact that this was a headquarters of a special police unit attached to the military, it was, in fact, a legitimate military target. We'll put aside the possibilities of collateral damage. But as purely a military target, you would agree that this is in fact a military target, a legitimate military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I'd like to clarify, just clarification on what the term "legitimate military target" means. Is there such a thing as an illegitimate military target? A military target presumably is a military target. Legitimate, I'm not sure if that is it intended to convey the method of attack is legitimate. I just want to be clear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will change it. And I think your intercession is probably an accurate criticism of the question, Judge, and I think we'll just go --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It was a military target, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to answer that question with yes but have the opportunity to say something extra to that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just -- if you sketch the situation, as you sketch it, it is, to my opinion, first of all, not possible to do what you say, set aside all the other things of collateral damage because whenever you judge a military target -- no, please, let explain me, because you use that as set aside the things of collateral damage. I cannot put that aside because in analysing a military target in a situation that was given in analysing a target was given to me with the information connected to it from the Office of the Prosecutor, I cannot disconnect it. If you sketch me a different situation, then I have to analyse that different situation carefully, and I cannot do that in one single minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, if we may, and I think that we have to segregate these questions, or I think this is going to take longer than it should. What you're talking about is the rule of proportionality, whether or not the military advantage gained is excessive in light of possible collateral damage. That is the rule of proportionality, is it not?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot answer it in that way because I'm talking about the information that is it given to me by the OTP where it says that, Housed approximately 30 members of Ministry of Interior special police who were attached to the military, not present prior to the artillery attack. Also housed Serb civilian refugees. I cannot, in all honesty, disconnect those factors given to me. If you come up with the fact that there was also ammunition found in that same building that adds extra factors to it. And then have you to analyse the situation all over again. But that can be -- that can have been the ammunition that belonging to the 30 soldiers. And then I keep asking myself the proportionality of attacking with artillery a church where civilian refugees were housed and the real -- the real advantage to be gained by destroying or by neutralizing that church. And by the way, I have never seen any effect mentioned anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the assessment -- two issues based on what you said, so the assessment that you made is based solely on the assumptions given to you by the OTP; and you did no independent assessment yourself on other facts that you may have come up with.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did it, first of all, by the -- on the information that was given me by the OTP, and on -- and including in that information was not only this list of targets but were also the operational orders from the Croatian forces in order to attack Knin, and in neither of those information I could find that extra information that I was looking for. And I do not doubt that in itself an ARSK special police headquarters is a military target. I do not doubt about that. But I do have serious questions about the fact that this target appears on a target list in -- with the name of only church without properly stating what it is, without properly stating the effect that you want to achieve, and I seriously have a problem with the fact that in that target, apparently there are civilian refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me stay with that. And your concern about civilian refugees goes to your concern about the possibility of civilian casualties if this entity should be hit and targeted and hit. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you aware or were you told prior to coming in here to testify last week that -- I'm referring to the report of Dr. Clark, P1251, that when he did the exhumation in the Knin cemetery, he could only account for one civilian that had died of a blast injury and possibly two. One, and this is at page 9 of his report, paragraph 2. Were you made aware of that fact when you came in here?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now that is a significant issue when assessing collateral damage, is it not, that whether or not there was something improper with this firing because you, when you're analysing this as an expert, have to examine the issue of a military target and weigh the advantage, the military advantage of hitting that target against potential excessive collateral damage.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there is more than only lethal collateral damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's just stay with the lethal. Lethal collateral damage means lives?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is that the most important collateral damage, lives?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I disagree with you. I disagree with you in the fact that collateral damage in large is, of course -- I'm sorry, I reacted too quickly. Yes, that is the most important thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when someone like General Gotovina is weighing the military advantage to be gained by hitting this entity, in this case the St. Ante's monastery, the ARSK special police headquarters, he has to weigh that possibility of collateral damage. But as you sit here, you are unaware of exactly what factors he was weighing when the decision was made to hit that entity. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was. Of course, I'm not aware of his -- of his way of thinking and the factors that he weighed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Knowing what you know now of what the chief pathologist medical examiner noted about one civilian death, and knowing that this was a headquarters of an entity that was supporting the army of the Republic of Serb Krajina, you would agree with me, would you not, Colonel, that a reasonable commander could come to a different conclusion in weighing those two items, come to a different conclusion on the propriety of attacking this target. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Not a question of who is right and who is wrong --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was thinking about it. Yes, I can follow you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you would agree that a reasonable commander could come to a different conclusion. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He can, of course, come to a different conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, could you explain to me how findings of a pathologist, of which this witness is not aware - or at least unless you tell me that you are - how many, where, what circumstances, the totality of his findings. But apart from lack of knowledge of that, how finally the number of blast victims could be something to have been taken into account prior to -- let's -- let me just try to explain to you what my problem is, so that you perhaps can deal with the matter. If I'm shelling - I'm not saying that this happened - in an area full of civilian population, and if for whatever reason they all had been down in their cellars by -- for whatever reason, and only one stayed upstairs, would that be a -- would that be -- would that allow for a final judgement on whether it was appropriate or not when we have only one victim? That's not the test would, it be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you're suggesting this more or less to a witness who has got no idea about what exactly Dr. Clark investigated, what the results were, what -- and you are asking him a judgement which is, as far as I can see now, is somewhat dependant on a lot of information where you more or less implicitly have criticised this witness for not taking into account information that was not presented to him, so he --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you're saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I want to be clear about that, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... No, it's perfectly clear that what you say is you can't form a full opinion on matters if you only have half the information. What we see now is that you're doing more or less exactly the same by giving a bit of information here, a bit of information there, and then ask the witness to draw conclusions on as much, perhaps a defective basis, as you say, he formed his opinion upon when he had only at his disposal the information given to him by the Prosecution. I just want you to be aware of what was on my mind so that you can take this into account in the continuation of your cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just one comment, and I will proceed quickly, which is the issue of collateral damage, and the Prosecutor did, in fact, bring forth questions before this witness on collateral damage issues and I -- I refer Your Honour to the direct examination when Mr. Russo presented information on P64 which was Lieutenant-Colonel Hjertnes' report that the collateral damage issues, and of course, did not present this witness fairly, I believe, with the rest of that information on collateral damages such as the information from Dr. Clark on the possible blast victims, civilian blast victims. Obviously there was some soldiers. Civilian blast victims. So when meeting what is presented by the Prosecution, I thought it was incumbent upon me in fairness to the witness to develop the story just a bit and give him some of the facts that have presented as a -- to this Chamber as early as last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now we can move on, Colonel, and -- we did talk a bit about the northern barracks, and I believe that in -- that's on page 1 of your document, and you noted in -- it's number -- page 1 of your addendum, number 2, on 2(c)(ii), you noted that was an item of low military value. That was, of course, before you were told that the headquarters of the 7th Krajina Corps was in the northern barracks, and that was in D928. That piece of information was not told to you. The other piece of information on that score, sir, is -- and if I could just bring up another item in P928. If we can go to D928, excuse me, D928. Again, this is a General Sekulic's book, and the fact you were told to assume was that there approximately 30 soldiers were manning medical facilities, kitchen, and a technical workshop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm trying to get the exact page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We'll come back to this exhibit when we find it. It was a provision I wanted to read you in D928, but we can find it and come back in a bit. The next item I wanted to talk to you about was the Knin police station, and you talk about that on --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Oh, you have it? Okay. Good. We're going back to P928 in the northern barracks, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That would be P61 in the English. In the middle paragraph: "The key units." In that second paragraph - if we can just blow that up a little bit - you see that, the "key units," Colonel?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "The key units in the special units corps were the armoured brigade and the guards brigade. Before the Oluja started the guards brigade and abandoned the combat assignment on Dinara. They abandoned Dinara without authorisation and assembled in the barracks in Knin where they were at the beginning of Oluja." Now, I take it from the facts that were given to you by the Prosecutor, you were not told that this special unit corps was in the northern barracks on the morning of the 4th?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not told to me by the OTP, and it's also not mentioned in the enemy paragraph of the operational order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the fact that this particular corps is there is a significant issue for individuals that are deciding whether to fire on this facility, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In case you assume that the corps, and I don't have information on the size, their weapon systems, their status, before attacking such a target, you need to know that as well, you understand. But take the assumption that a corps -- that a -- sorry, a brigade from a certain size and strength is located in northern barracks, that changes the situation and then you need a new analysis on that situation, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now you could conclude, could you not, that -- well, let me withdraw that. A reasonable commander could conclude, could he not, that in firing on the northern barracks his fire could very well deter or suppress the activity of this special unit. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that straightforward because as I said before I do not know what is the composition of that brigade how many soldier it were. What was their status, what was their armament, what were their intentions. Only if I have proper information on that, that is the proper information that a reasonable commander would require in order to judge whether he will use his artillery against the northern barracks, yes or no. And without all those information that you -- that a reasonable commander would use, I don't think I can answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, given the fact that you have learned since have you been here that the northern barracks was the headquarters of the 7th Krajina Corps and was there on the morning of the 4th and that the -- this special unit was located there, that you heard evidence that artillery -- the chief artillery officer for the ARSK couldn't get anybody to drive him into town because of that fire. Would you not agree, based on the facts that you heard, that this was a military target of very significant value?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received information from various sides. I have received information from the OTP which says that there is no headquarter in that barracks, that there are only a few soldiers there manning the barracks. That's one point, one side of the information. If I look in the operational order from -- for the Operation Storm, and if I look in the paragraph of -- which is stating what the -- what the enemy is, I cannot find the information on the presence of the 7th, HQ, ARSK in Knin, in the northern barracks. There is no detailed information on that. So, given --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I really need to stop you, sir, because I really have a limited time. My question for you on line 20 was that -- and would you or would you not agree based on the facts that you heard that this being the northern bearings was a military target of very significant value. Would you agree with that, or would you not?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, I cannot answer that with a straight no or yes because you don't give me the information that I require to give you that answer. If you give me that information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Konings, Mr. Kehoe is asking you whether on the basis of the information you have now, whether on the basis of that information, you would consider it to be a military target of very significant value. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... of course, if you would have other information, you might come to a different conclusion, but that is what he is asking you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think it's -- it's a military target of high value.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's move on, sir, and we'll talk about the Knin police station that you referred to in -- page 2, number 17, of your addendum. Now, the Chamber has received evidence that approximately 550 police officers were deployed on various positions on the Dinara and that their communication between these officers on the front line and officers in the Knin police station, until those -- there was communication between those officers on the front line an officers in the Knin police station until those communications were knocked out by Croatian forces. Your Honour, I can give the record transcript cites for this, but I would have to go into private session just briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, when you came to your conclusion that the targeting of the Knin police station was of no military value, did you consider that these police officers were participating in the -- in the ARSK defence up on the Dinara and that they were communicating back to their headquarters in Knin? Did you consider that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me one second, please. No, I had no idea -- I had no information that they were communicating with the police forces in the Dinara area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Then let us explore this just a little bit more. Before that -- we go into private session for another question, would you agree that it would be to the military advantage of the HV to attack a headquarters that was in communication with their soldiers; in this case, police officers, on the front line. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you -- in case you -- no, let's assume you classify those ten police officers being a headquarters, which I -- which -- that information was not given to me, then I think that is -- well, attacking such a headquarters can -- can be of military advantage, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. And it is, in fact, 550 policemen that were operating as soldiers not 110.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I just want to clarify about that. I believe the witness is referring to the number of policemen he believes were in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us take this one step further on the military advantage gained, and just briefly again in private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, if we can turn to D923. Without addressing ourselves to the individual, you didn't know that those communications between the police and the soldiers on the front line were knocked out or were lost on roughly 10.00, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know that -- I did not though that. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is it an assessment on the screen by General Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 6 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in that paragraph that notes: "The Ustasha breakthrough over the Dinara mountains during the afternoon of the 4th of August represented the greatest threat for the collective activities of the 7th corps." And I will tell you that's the 7th Krajina Corps part of the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. The "the MUP" the MUP being the Ministry of Interior. " The MUP special unit leaving its positions on the Dinara around 1100 offered the Ustasha forces a possibility for a swift breakthrough over the Dinara mountains towards Crvena Zemlja." Now, if we can take this sequentially, sir, we have a headquarters that is operating in support of -- or in excess of 500 soldiers a headquarters that is manned by policemen, communications are lost on the 10th, and thereafter, on the -- at approximately -- excuse me, communications are lost at 1000 hours. At 1100 hours this special unit breaks and left its position giving the HV a significant breakthrough on the Dinara. Would you agree, based on this additional information which you didn't have, that the targeting of the police headquarters offered a significant military advantage to the HV?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: By saying that, you should guess that there is a direct connection between the targeting of the headquarters and the leaving of the MUP special unit of the front line, and I cannot say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So are you telling me that you make no connection between the loss of communications at 1000 hours with the police headquarters and the -- as General Mrksic says, the MUP, the MUP special unit leaving its position on Dinara mountains at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's one of the possibilities. I tried to -- to take into, to bear in mind that in a military world in operations, there is might be several other solutions or several other possibilities. One other thing is, one observation that I offer you is that those MUP special units operating in the front line were apparently embedded inside other military units and must have had contact with other military units as well or being under command of other military units. So there might be, and I know I'm getting into the speculation area, there might have been other solutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not get into speculation for whatever reason. Your answer is clear, you say this -- there may have been a causal relationship. I might not have sufficient information to come to a final conclusion on this. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might have just one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm reminded of one issue, sir, you noted -- did you not say that during the reviewing, General Gotovina's attack order that there was no mention that these Special Forces were going back -- that the special forces were in Knin, and then when we were talking about the northern barracks.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was mention that I said -- or it was mentioned that some of the special forces were there, but the words "headquarters," there is no detailed information. The paragraph on enemy is very, very generic, and it doesn't give you any detail that I would expect to be connected to an operational order. It gives something like there were 800 conscripts inside the city of Knin. But I do not have any specific information. So you may be right that the headquarters was there. I do not have the information. I cannot read it from the operational order, nor do I find an annex to the operational order, which in a NATO situation, we have an annex to an operational order, the annex Bravo, which describes the exact disposition of the enemy as you know them. So if have you the information that several HQs are up and running inside the Knin of Knin, I was looking to find that information somewhere specified. I couldn't. Maybe you have that information, but I couldn't find it in the information begin to me by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We'll get to that in a little bit more detail in a bit, but I would like to finish some of the targets you have assessed.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And let's go back to the list and talk a little bit the Senjak barracks which is of course on P1271 as KV 350. And I take it you were told to assume that the logistics base housing main logistics staff - I take this from your addendum - and it also had some government offices. Now, let me show you some of the activity that took place on that day. And were you informed about actually what was transpiring or given a field for what was transpiring at the Senjak barracks on the 4th?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure, but maybe Your Honour can help me out what the word transpiring exactly means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That was taking place.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That was takes place at the Senjak barracks?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Because I don't see any in the actual facts as they were presented to you. Were you told orally or in any fashion what was going on at the Senjak barracks?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's just touch on a couple of them. And if we go first to D61 which is the diary of the chief logistics officer for the ARSK, senior officer Bjelanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: D161. I'm sorry. D161, I apologise if I misspoke in that fashion -- any fashion. If we can go to page 6 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this is one of the entries for the 4th of August where he -- that Bjelanovic notes at 1640 -- and by the way, it is page 5 in the B/C/S -- page 5 in the B/C/S. But at 1620: "I went to the rear command post Senjak barracks, had a short meeting with senior officers and deployed those [sic] senior officers to various items -- to various tasks?" He finishes that: "This way I reduced the burden for the rear command post. Practically there were no conditions for work." One other fact I'd like to bring to your attention is D923. Again, this is General Mrksic's report. And if we can go to page 24 of 29. If we could just scroll down a bit more on that page, certainly in the English. And again General Mrksic is talking about the activities on the 4th. He notes in paragraph 3: "Due to incessant activity of the enemy artillery and rocket system, from the Senjak barracks in Knin, where at the ... beginning of the attack, three trucks had been destroyed and a driver... killed. It was not possible to carry out any relocation of quartermaster or any other materiel supplies." Now, I take it you were not given that information either, prior to coming here. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen this document, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that information was provided in a hypothetical during direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The question was about another stage. That is, prior to coming to court. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And maybe that question was not as precise as I might have wanted, Colonel. The question I have, prior to you writing your report or coming here to testify, you did not have this information, did you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now would you agree with me that now that you know that there was activity - for instance, deploying forces - and that as a result of the -- the deploying officers in any event. As a result of firing on this Senjak barracks, the ARSK was unable to move supplies, would you agree, sir, that the firing on the Senjak barracks offered a significant military advantage to the HV?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the sentences that you showed me are not given that implication completely, because it doesn't say that this Senjak barracks was apparently what you are suggesting, a main army supply area. It says any relocation of quartermaster or any other materiel supplies, in which area? In the whole region of the ARSK? Does it mean that -- what you are saying that by attacking the Senjak barracks that the whole supply system of the ARSK in that area collapsed? Because that is what you are suggesting. That is what you are saying to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is a very simple question. Based on the information that you now know, number 1, that the head logistics office of Bjelanovic was meeting there and deploying officers to various tasks. But more importantly as a result of the attack or the firing on the Senjak barracks, it was impossible to carry out any relocation of a quartermaster or materiel supplies.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In itself, that sentence doesn't say anything to me, unless you can tell me what exactly is meant. Is it meant relocation of quartermaster and other materiel supplies in which area, to which forces? In the whole area of the ARSK, or in a limited area? Because that is of significant importance to know that in order to be able to analyse the new information and to analyse whether it is a very valuable target which contributes to -- to the -- to the defeat of a force. If this is a main supply base, and if -- assume that this is a main supply base and assume that the artillery attack is capable of neutralizing this main supply base, well, that gives -- sheds another light on the situation, and I don't read that information in that paragraph, that you -- that you show me here. That's the only thing I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, you know that the Senjak barracks is the main supply facility for the 7th Krajina Corps. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says it is a rear logistic HQ. So if that means that it is the main supply for the 7th HQ, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Are you saying to this Court that firing on the main supply depot for the 7th Krajina Corps to disrupt and suppress their ability to move supplies, are you saying that that is not enough to -- for you to conclude that attacking the Senjak barracks on the 4th of August offered a military advantage to the HV? Are you saying that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that. I ask you a question for further information in the way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No -- I'm willing to answer yes, so I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that you should say yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I was preparing to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is a question which includes the significance of this target. Now what we hear from you is that to say that get reliable assessment on the significance would have to know more. It's on the basis of information which is of a not precise nature. I have difficulties in coming to a conclusion that it was significant in this sense, as you include in your question. That seems to be an answer to your question, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Colonel once again, on a reasonable commander standard, you would agree that a reasonable commander could assess these facts concerning the Senjak barracks, and its -- the fact that is the main supply depot for the 7th Krajina Corps. You could assess those facts and could conclude that, A, attacking that would offer a significant military advantage; and that, B, the only thing he had to do after that was assess whether or not the value of that attacking and taking -- hitting that target was outweighed by potential collateral damage. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that is a weighing process -- that's a weighing process that a reasonable commander does, and conclusions one way or the other can differ?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us turn to your next target, which is the ARSK main headquarters. And let us first talk about the ARSK main headquarters, which is the -- the main headquarters in the defence ministry. Now, I want to -- we've been talking to some degree when we were at the 7th Krajina Corps about the targets at an operational level, and even when we were talking about the movements of the 4th Guards Brigade and the 7th Guards Brigade, we were operating at the operational and the tactical level. I would like to take this one step further and talk to you about the strategic level. And you know the difference, the strategic level being the most significant level moving from the macro to the micro. Isn't that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So we go from strategic operational, tactical?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the most strategic target in the Republic of Serbian Krajina for the ARSK was their main headquarters in Knin, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that is so because this is the place that the ARSK conducted their war efforts throughout the Krajina, right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So hitting a strategic target of that fashion could offer a significant military advantage to the HV, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you'd noted for us that there are -- and I note back in your report, there are many reasons for artillery. And I'm talking about page 2 of P1259. And one of those is suppression, another one is interdiction, another one is harassment, and other one is destroy. Now, attacking a headquarters such as the ARSK, it is a valid intent of the commander to attack that facility, not necessarily to destroy it, but to, as you say on page 2 of your first report, to neutralise the headquarters, suppress activity in that headquarters, and harass the command and control functions of the ARSK. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And those are all legitimate goals of artillery as you described in your report, putting aside any effort to destroy that facility.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now that, of course, as you noted, would -- because of its strategic value, would make this a very significant target.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in combat situations, the enemy cannot protect a target, a strategic target of this value, merely by placing that target in a civilian-populated area, can they? Because if that were the case, nobody would be able to fire on such a target. They can't do that, can they? And if you say they can, tell me where you find your written support for that.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would like to answer that question in saying that this happens, not only here but all over the world. These kind of targets are placed inside the middle of civilian-populated areas, and I'm not the one to judge whether that is legal, illegal, or whatever. I have a personal opinion about that, but I leave that for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So what you're telling me is you can't answer that question?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir. And at any point you say you can't answer the question, I don't want to take you out of your field of expertise. Let us turn to another set of targets, and that would be the railroad-related targets. And basically I'm looking at the targets that are in your addendum, and I'm -- looking at them jointly as railroad targets 13, 14. I believe those are the ones that we're talking about here. I'll collectively refer to them. And you basically say that -- let me answer that. The information that you were given about there railroad targets if we could go back in here and turn to page 12, you basically say that there was no use being made of these railroad facilities, is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information that was given to me doesn't state any actual use of the railroad system during that days [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you a document that was presented by the Office of the Prosecutor in P804, and this is an ECMM report of the 4th of August of 1995.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could bring that up on the screen. And if we could go down to item 4.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you can see that -- under economical, industrial, and infrastructural. "Obviously a lot of damage during the day. Trains are seen ... moving in Knin ... presumably used for military purpose, but could these be used for the evacuation of civilians?" Now, I take it based on information that you were given that you weren't told that the Prosecutor had introduced evidence that trains were, in fact, moving?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am a going to object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: First of all, putting to the witness that the Prosecution put in particular evidence doesn't seem to me to be anything other than attempting to convince the witness that he should adopt whatever is put in front of him. In any case --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can I answer that, Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, if you would it -- if you would ask the witness whether he was aware of or whether he was informed about, let's then forget about all the underlying and implicit suggestion of what was appropriate or not, and then we -- because that's what we want to hear from the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of this information, so I was not aware of moving trains.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's talk a little bit more about the movement and the use of trains. I referred just earlier in the cross, I believe on Friday, concerning the ARSK's military supply depot at Golubic and the train station nearby. And if I could just refer you to, if I may, again, back to D923, page 23 of 29. And just towards -- if we could just scroll up just a bit. We're talking about the relocation of materiel supplies. The General writes that: "Relocation of materiel supplies especially ammunition and mines and explosives store Golubic ... the activities were carried out in three directions. Establishing a field store in Tiskovac tunnels, establishing a mobile ammunition store on the railway wagons, and relocation of part of ammunition from Golubic to the store Cerkezovac in Banja area. "The fall of Glava on 28 July and the Ustasha attack on the communications Strmica-Golubic-Knin slowed down the activities on relocation of the store." If I can just flip ahead a few more dates. If we can go to page 25 of this document, and we'll bring it into focus for activities as reported by the General Mrksic in Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can just scroll up the bottom. I want to start there on 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "On 5 August," that would be the second day of storm: "1995 in the morning, the organs of the Main Staff logistics found themselves in Srb where they established a rear command post and made an overview of the logistics support system functioning. Then it was ordered to evacuate 14 railway wagons loaded with ammunition from the tunnel on the axis of Stara Straza - Padjene and to relocate them to Otric Malovan region in order to take them to Republika Srpska territory." Now, before I go on to the next sentence, Colonel, are you familiar with these tunnels and their close proximity to downtown Knin?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were tunnels. I have seen themselves in Knin, but I do not recall the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. In these tunnels that were located around Knin, did you know that they were loaded with ammunition?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go on. "However the train personnel in the security left the wagons during night, but even if they had been at their work posts in the morning, it would not have been possible to do anything constructive since Malovan had already been under enemy fire." Next paragraph down: "In order to initiate destruction of ammunition in the tunnels near Stara Straza, the armoured train" -- By the way, are you familiar with the armoured train that the ARSK had?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "The armoured train was pushed in order to insight an explosion due to the inertia and crashed with the wagons loaded with ammunition. This operation failed because the train turned over before the entry into the tunnel. "It was ordered to blow up to the mined ammunition store Golubic and for that all preparations had been carried out previously. But due to the disruption of the communications it was not possible to forward this order to the store commander." Now, if, in fact, Colonel, the ARSK was using these railway lines to move ammunition, and if, in fact, there was some activity in these railway lines on the 4th, you would you agree with me that the HV could achieve a significant military advantage by attacking those rail lines and preventing the ARSK from moving any of this ammunition. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is -- that is right. But I think it's -- no, that's right. I leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm about to move into my last subject on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President. I don't know if you want to take a break now, or do you want me to conclude?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Depends on how much time you need for the last subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't think it will take too long. If we can just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Too, too long. It could be 5 or 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It would be five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five minutes, and that would be your --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That would be the last part on this particular segment before I move to a completely different topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then if you would use your next five minutes to complete the subject, and after the break we'll move on with another one. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The next topic -- target I would like to talk to you about, sir, is the telegraph and post office that you referred to in the -- number 14 where you note it is not a military target. The first issue is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can just briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can put 1D65-0519 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is an multi-page document, Colonel, that was written by General Mrksic or signed by General Mrksic, the head of the ARSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will tell you on dating, Mr. President, just so I can date this. The difficulty with dating this is that there is no date on the document per se. We do know it is signed by General Mrksic, and we do know that General Mrksic took over as head of the ARSK approximately mid-May of 1995. So in the context we know it's thereafter. I wish I could hone it down more precisely, Mr. President, but that's the best can I do with this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we look at this document, and we go down to the third paragraph, and -- actually -- the means of communication. Do you see that Colonel?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "The means of communication that the SVK," which is the army of the Serb Krajina, "has at its disposition based at the PTT," post and telecommunications and the railway, "it is possible to secure only 40 per cent of the necessary communications for the purpose [sic] of command information and cooperation. So you would you agree with me, Colonel, that based on this, it would appear that the ARSK is running at least some of their communications through the PTT facility?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is stated here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And as a consequence of that, it would make this facility or a military target, and knocking out that facility would quite possibly give a military advantage to the HV. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have to go back to what I said before. This is a mixture of military and civilian issues inside one target, and if you put the question forward like that, I cannot answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, again on that score, the ARSK military cannot immunise their assets by mixing them with civilian asset, can they? Immunise their assets from attack by mixing them with civilian assets, can they?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You cannot completely immunise -- you cannot completely immunise by putting military targets and combine them with civilian property or civilians. And again then you come back to the answer that I gave before, then you come in a combination of military issues or military assets with civilian assets, and attacking such a combination of issues, military and civilian, brings you into a -- assessment of the situation that has to be done by the appropriate commander on the scene, and that might be either, in certain cases, the tactical commander or that might be even the strategical commander in order to decide to attack that specific target, yes or no. And then what we discussed before, you come back to proportionate damage, collateral damage, the value of that target. And with -- having said that, well, I cannot give you any further -- further explanation on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Apparently, you can envision a significant military advantage to the HV to knock out the communication facilities that the PTT that was used by the ARSK. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would not say not at all cost because I do think there are other possibilities. There are more telegraph headquarters. If you want to knock down that specific facility against all cost, that is the decision of the tactical or operational commander of the attacking force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How many PTT facilities are there in Knin?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were more, I think. Was also a railway -- a railway system. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There was one main facility, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'd like to offer into evidence 1D65-0519.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1262.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit D1262 is admitted into evidence. We'll have a break, and we will resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I was informed that you would like to address me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and the Chamber. I just wanted to follow-up, Mr. President, on your comments concerning the collateral damage of civilians, and my understanding as part of the Prosecution's case was a presentation at least through P64 of the collateral damage as assessed by Lieutenant-Colonel Hjertnes. Of course that is just one portion of the collateral damage. The other portion of the collateral damage is obviously the human, collateral damage and in this case injuries. And in assessing whether or not this particular attack violated the rule of proportionality, of course the assessment is whether or not the military advantage was outweighed by the excessive damage to civilians and property and civilian property. And I trust that part of the assessment that was made by Prosecution in showing P64 was at least some degree presenting that type of evidence to support the argument that their collateral damage was, in fact, excessive. To counter that in part, and of course we will address the other aspect, the damage to the property, account of that in part, is assessment of the civilian costs involved in Operation Storm. And as we know from Dr. Clark the -- Dr. Clark was only able to ascertain one civilian death from blast injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kehoe, the main reason I intervened at that moment and to that extent, I think your comparison with what was done by Mr. Russo in relation to the -- to the -- to Hjertnes is that the first question Mr. Russo put to the witness is, Have you read this report? That was your first question. Now, to put to a witness a document which he is, A, not aware of; B, has apparently has no idea who was in graves, how many graves were. And then to say one blast injury, it could be -- Mr. Kehoe, let's be clear, I think an attack even without any casualty could be inappropriate, whereas in other cases where you have casualties, more than one, it could be that such an attack was -- was legitimate by objective, by means, et cetera, and we all know it's -- it's a complex question. So what I was addressing was to put something to a witness who has no idea about the document neither about the context and to put one conclusion to him and then to seek to elicit from him conclusions on the basis of that, and that is something -- and that's the reason why I told you that that doesn't assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not to say that -- that there was only one blast victim, casualty. I can imagine that that's important for you. It is about the way in which you use this information and how you present this to the witness. I think that I -- and the Chamber has been critical and even in the observations, I think I not only have some words for you, but I think I also addressed at the same time the Prosecution on -- that's the reason why I raised the issue not to say that it's an irrelevant fact but whether it should be put to a witness who has got no idea about the context, whereas it's a rather complex matter and whereas the questions, the legal questions involved, should be carefully analysed not be mixed up with what could the expectations -- expectations and result is not the same thing. Sometimes you can have very good expectations and the result can be very bad. It could be the other way around. Now what role do expectations play in the legal context, and again, it is not -- it is not perhaps directly applicable. I'm not expressing any opinion on that, but for the framework of mind, Protocol I of course gives quite some guidance for thinking on these matters, and I'm not always fully convinced by the way in which the questions are put in relation to the legal analyse that should be underlying these type of questions because if you don't have a clear analytical legal view on the matters then questions, possible consequences, causal relationships, appropriate, inappropriate, what is an objective, is the objective the same as a target? All these questions might become blurred, and that would be my concern, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate the concern, and I know that it's a difficult assessment, and I appreciate what Your Honour says that a completely legitimate attack could, in fact, cause significant collateral damage and vice versa, a otherwise illegal attack could cause little or no damage and still nonetheless be illegal if the possibility was excessive. That being said, of course, the analysis of and the after-the-fact analysis of an attack certainly takes into mind or calls to mind the human cost that is involved, and I -- I do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then you have to know the context in order to form an opinion on --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm giving him the context that was given to us by the Office of the Prosecutor. That's the context. The context is Dr. Clark. And that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not further argue about whether that is a proper and sufficient context. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I just wanted some clarity on it before I moved into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I hope I have given that clarity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will stay off the subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I just want to put something on the record. The Court had asked the Prosecution to find an unredacted version of Exhibit P1272. This was a target list that had what appeared to be a redaction on it. I indicated to the Court that those were highlights. I have now been informed that the highlighted version which you can read is actually the original in the Croatian archive. What was sent to us and what is in our evidence room is also a copy with redactions, so we will request the original. It will take some time in order to bring to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have been presented with a highlight, my, and I think the Chamber's main problem, is we couldn't read. So if you make a photocopy in colour or something like that so that you can distinguish between the yellow or the green and what is the text below it then --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's correct, judge, we just need to get the actual highlighted copy from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have received it in this --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's correct, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you can't read it, then it is very difficult to translate it, isn't it? Must be someone who has been able to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm not sure if those particular lines have been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, they were not translated. I apologise for this mistake. Try to get them as soon as possible. Then I have one other issue that is -- I think last week we, Monday, I think it was, we briefly discussed any further admissions on what we call the Pittman letter. Now I said that if possible any further submissions to be made within still this week. Now this week is -- it was not a very firm deadline, but it was guidance to the parties --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. We thought you meant within one week, and we are filing that today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that's therefore -- is that clear to the other Defence counsel as well that the Chamber expects now not if possible anymore but within a week, and we made a week now seven days so that the deadline is today. Thank you. Any other procedural matters? If not, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Konings, Mr. Kehoe will continue his cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, just a couple of clarifying questions. Prior to the 4th of August of 1995, you did not review any evidence that the HV had been firing any types of artillery into Knin, had you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. And that was a situation that was very different from what you observed in Sarajevo, where there was a regular firing into Sarajevo by the Bosnian Serbs, right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Likewise, sir, that you would agree with me, one of the ways that a military commander can attempt to ensure that collateral damage to civilians is limited is by commencing an attack at a time when he may believe that there would be very few civilians on the street. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, seems to be a fair conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in this particular instance, the attack on Knin commenced at 5.00 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the artillery attack?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The artillery attack commenced at 5.00 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But lasts for more than 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My questions to you was the did -- the initial artillery attack commenced at 5.00, did it not?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did you receive -- did you receive information at the time that there was literally no civilians on the street at 5.00 a.m. on the morning of the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not received specific detailed information which was saying either one or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, isn't it a notorious fact that the -- unless there is any exceptional circumstance that at 4.00 in the morning there are considerably less people in the streets than during normal day-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
