utterances.text: The only issue, Judge, is making a record on that issue. I know Your Honour appreciates that. Nevertheless for the benefit of those -- if hopefully not that may read that at some point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if is a notorious fact, you can introduce it in argument as a notorious fact, and then there is no reason to present any evidence. But of course, very theoretically speaking you could as yourself whether Mr. Konings has taken this into consideration when forming his opinions on the matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, did you know there was, in fact, that there was a curfew in Knin?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. So you couldn't help us with the hours or anything like that --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to talk about your alternative plan. In your report you disagree with the tactics employed by the HV, and you lay out a different plan or a different alternative --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. The transcript is not running.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was just trying to get it run, and it apparently is -- mine stops at page 47, line 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The transcript is working on the middle monitor for us, Your Honour, but not on our individual screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that is where I was looking at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was informed that it is a general problem in this courthouse with the LiveNote server which will be re-booted from what I understand. Since the other screen works, I suggest that we continue up to the moment where we have to scroll back and where we are finding problems in referring to earlier portions of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before we move on, Colonel, I'd like to just follow up on -- on your comment just now where you noted that while the attack commenced at 5.00 a.m., it continued throughout the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I could call up 1D65-0512.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, this is the meteorological forecast for -- it should be August. And if we look at -- obviously there is nothing for Knin. If we look at Zagreb -- excuse me, if we look at Gospic and Split for the 4th, we note that the sunrise was at 5.48. Now, that's also for Split. Is it 5.47, but we're talking, you know, approximately quarter to, ten to 6.00. Now, the video that we examined during the course of your direct examination, you noted that when it was still dark, what was had was what you described as harassment fire. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The part of the video that we saw, yes, that was a kind of, yeah, harassment interdiction fire, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the initial barrage of fire was over by that point, wasn't it? And what we had after that was what you termed to be harassment fire?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now if we could move this into evidence, Mr. President. 1D65-0512.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D12634, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it is admitted into evidence. I could have imagined that parties would have stipulated that the sun went up quarter to 6.00. But if we need documents for this, then fine. Is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, what I'd like to explore with you at this point was your alternative plan and what you maintain that the HV should have done as opposed to conducting the artillery attack in Knin and up in the Dinara and elsewhere in conjunction with the infantry fighting. And I'd like to turn your attention to page 4, and this is your addendum, 3(A)(i). It goes from page 4 over to page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this is -- for the record this is in P1260.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can read that just briefly. I think you have that with you, sir.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "With the exception of the shelling of two or three military targets," see analysis, "the use of artillery against the city of Knin is of no direct military essence of limited effectiveness and could have been avoided by entering the city with combat troops from various different directions, having the information that there would be practically no defence. The 4th Guards Brigade that had received the order to take control of the city counted around 1900 personnel. And can be classified to be a larger combat unit capable of taking control of the city by means of a fast, well coordinated, and controlled action. Doing so, collateral damage to civilians than their property could have been minimised as much as possible." Now, just taking that last sentence, "doing so, collateral damage to civilians and their appropriate could have been minimised as much as possible." You don't, in fact, don't know what that collateral damage was, if any, do you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm interested in various portions of your proposal, and I'm interested in the information that you had. And I want to start with that sentence that you noted that: "That the HV could have avoided -- by entering the city with combat troops from various directions." Now, you told us last week that you looked at the 4th Guards Brigade, but that you didn't analyse the activities of the 7th Guards Brigade. What other directions are you talking about? What information did you have upon which you based your conclusion that they could have entered the city from various directions?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have specific information. I know the general direction that the Croatian troops were coming from, which was from -- I have to recall that roughly, north, north-east. But doing such an approach to a city, a commander has the possibility to explore the surrounds, the environment, of Knin and could have been offered the possibilities to enter the city from more than one side because there are more roads running into the city. And I'm not trying to explain here a complete solution. I only try to offer a possibility that is described in our doctrine that when you have the task in taking control of a urban environment, in this case, Knin, that the preference is there to do that in a, let's put it in a way, in a -- in an action of surprise, where you use your weapon system in a minimum as possible. And, of course, when it's a heavily defended city with defence lines on the outside that then you take another direction. What I've tried to do here is offer you -- offer the Court a generic idea about an alternative, not based on specific detailed information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, before we continue, the LiveNote computer has been re-booted. Everyone can connect again so that you can use both screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can I just continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the fact is, Colonel, when Operation Storm began, HV troops faced stiff resistance throughout the area from the ARSK, didn't they, on the front line?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did. But I was also reading in the information that I had that they were able to breakthrough that stiff resistance quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And which units was able to breakthrough the stiff resistance on the 4th.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- I cannot recall whether -- I'm not quite sure that the 7th Brigade already went through the resistance on the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the 7th Brigade stopped at Pljesevica on the 4th, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you don't know who, if any unit got through on the 4th, do you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that not what I suggest here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm asking that you question, sir.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to P698. And this is a report from Captain Dangerfield who was a sector liaison officer in UN Sector South. And I'd like to just talk you -- have you seen this report before, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not going to read through the whole thing. But if we go to -- this is it an assessment of what is transpired on the 4th with 2200 hours as the time. Do you see the top line there, sir? Brief overview for Sector South for 04, 0500 Bravo to 04, 2200 Bravo, August 1995. He notes in paragraph 2 -- he talks about the attack in paragraph 1. "It was a long time before the HV/HVO made any headway on the ground." He talks about the areas of attack. In number 3: "By mid-afternoon there were five main axes of attack." But let us turn to assessment in paragraph 10 which is the next page. "Saturday 05 August should see another initial heavy artillery barrage of HV objectives. G2 assessment is that Knin may fall by dark 05 ... in order [sic] to do so, I believe that the HV will require a more successful day than today. Troops approaching from the south face a stiff opposition." Now what is that stiff opposition that the HV was facing in the south?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you get any information - and this is SLO reccys last week so considerable evidence of road use by ARSK tracked vehicles? Those are mechanised units be they tanks, APC's, et cetera; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you have any idea of the amount of track vehicles the ARSK had and where they were deployed?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Paragraph 11: "In the west HV advances face problems of indirect major routes and that times difficult terrain in the approaches towards Knin. With the reports being unclear on the successes of these axes of advance and the distance still required to cover it -- to cover, it is unlikely that Knin will come under direct fire from them." Now, tell me about the problems in the west of the HV advance and how it was stalled on the 4th.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this -- this report describes that there were heavy problems, but I have no details about that. I haven't got the information, so I cannot tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, going back to your report, if I said that combat troops could have entered the city from various directions, and maybe you weren't provided this information, I trust you weren't. If you -- combat troops were supposed to come in from various directions, wouldn't it be important to know what type of resistance the various units of the HV encountered as the attack ensued?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement that I made in my report, as I tried to explain before but maybe I was not quite clear is that I offered you a -- that I offered a possibility to be used as an alternative. Which is described in our doctrine is you try to take a city, take control of a city without using any heavy weapon system in doing a kind of surprise action early in the morning, in the night, and -- let's put it in a way that is a kind of theoretical approach. I did not connect that to any information to the troops outside the city of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What you're advocating as this alternative is dispense with an artillery attack and engage in a full frontal infantry attack, pushing the ARSK lines further and further back towards Knin, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Looking to the situation that I was trying to depict for myself is that you see on a certain moment in time, and that may have been on the 5th, that the 7 Brigade broke through the lines of the enemy, that the 4th Brigade came in line with the 7th Brigade and that both brigades were directed together towards Knin. And from there you can think about the situation that you -- that you try to enter the city as soon as possible in one quick push without using -- without using any further artillery barrage at all. Seeing the fact that there was no communated [sic] combined defence and that to the information given to me, there were hardly any -- that there was resistance possible in Knin. I just offered that as a possibility and the commander on the spot has made his own choices based upon the actual information that he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, were you made aware of what the ARSK plans were for the defence of Knin?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's explore that just a bit and see if it will factor into your equation as to what was planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: By the way, do you know who General Commander Kovacevic is for the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can just go into private session, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We turn to P923 [sic] at page 3. Excuse me, D923. If I said P, D923, at page 3. I'm interested in the "aggression was expected --" No, just down in the middle paragraph. There we go. This is General Mrksic talking: "The aggression was expected, and the Main Staff directed the main focus of their work on preparing the units to defend their positions regions and areas resolutely for five to seven days, believing that that would be enough for the international factors, and, if necessary, even the Yugoslav army, to react ..." Did you know, sir, that that was the plan of the ARSK should they be attacked?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't -- I haven't read this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn your attention to D106. Now D106 that comes on the screen, colonel, is a radio interview with General Mrksic on the 4th of August, at 2130 hours with Radio Belgrade. And to the question second -- one, two, third down: "Does that mean our lines have been penetrated? Mrksic says: "No. We are maintaining contact; our forces withdrew to the positions for the direct defence of Knin." One last entry before we talk about this, and that would be D28, General Sekulic's book. And if I can call 928, D928 -- excuse me, it's D928. And if can I call 1D44-0119 in the English, and 1D44-0029 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have been told by my case manager it's page 24 in the English and page 27 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that 2000 hours meeting -- Colonel, that I just want to address you to that 2000 hours paragraph. There is a meeting at the Main Staff. Without reading the whole matter, midway down it notes that Commander Mrksic's position that the evacuation was a matter for the authorities indicates that: "The army ought to continue with defence and facilitate the evacuation of the population. The commander also decided to narrow the fronts of defence and continue with decisive defence. This was to apply to all corps. "In order to defend Knin, the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina Main Staff ordered that the commander of the 7th corps, General Kovacevic to" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "To pull out of the 75th brigade by morning and deploy it in positions for the defence of Knin at Bulina Strana." I will tell you that Bulina Strana is that bluff that we talked about just right above Knin. Now are you familiar with this term "decisive defence?"

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't use the term "decisive defence," but I have a -- I think I understand what is meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what do you think is meant?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Decisive defence, well, I would like to use another name. It can be seen as -- no, the defence has to take place in such a way that -- that it brings the decision in either a specific battle or an operation. And for the defending party that means that when it goes the wrong direction that the battle or the operation is lost. That's quite clear. That's my recollection from decisive defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And would it also the decisive defence be what we read before, a defence that it was down to the last man?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a recollection from the nation or the army involved. I don't think that that applies to -- to every army in the world because decisive defence can also mean that a reasonable commander or a commander decides when he sees that his operation is not successful anymore, in order to spare lives or further destruction that he decides either to withdraw or to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So it would be, if we can go back to P698, paragraph 15. Again, this is a Captain Dangerfield's comment. And go to paragraph 15, the last page. Second sentence in: "With the advancing HV/HVO troops looking at Knin as their final objective and ARSK -- Let me pull that up first. Paragraph 12 is at the top of the page. I'll read that first: "While Knin may come under heavy artillery attack again, the considerable presence of ARSK forces in the area will require more time before they come under direct fire from HV tanks." Now let's go back down to paragraph 15. "With the advancing HV/HVO troops looking at Knin as their final objective and ARSK troops remaining, Milan Martic will have to surrender or face a bloody last stand in the capital of Krajina." Now, when you engage, Colonel, in an option for a decisive defence, those are your two options: Surrender or a bloody last stand. Aren't they?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is another option, which is withdraw and leave the city as an open city. Withdrawal is always an option. Surrender is an option, withdrawal is an option and fighting to the last man is also a option.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what I read to you about these parties and the comments from the witness that I read to you concerning the decisive defence, there was discussion among the ARSK as relayed about the witness that I talked to you about fighting to the last man. And General Mrksic, as noted by General Kovacevic told his troops at 2000 hours on the 4th, to continue with the decisive defence. Now, with that information, you, as a senior military officer would conclude that the ARSK intended to make their last stand in Knin. Didn't they.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not said. Because a decisive defence can also take -- it is not necessary that a decisive defence will be taken indirectly in the city because as in Knin the environment offers perfect opportunities to make a choice and to do your decisive defence outside the city, because everybody knows that drawing a battle into a city will cause a lot of trouble, not only for the attacking party but also for the defensive party. And a decisive defensive can, of course, be related directly to the city itself, but it can also be built up in depth around the city using the terrain outside the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go into that because what you're talking about is the concept of fighting in built-up areas, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you fight up in built-up areas, the advantage in fighting in built-up areas is the defender, not the attacker; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the defender has a better advantage in a city if you can call that advantage at all, but, yes, he is probably in a better position than the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And let's go through some of the reasons for that. Because when you are talking about three's troops walking into Knin, you're essentially -- and you refer this to your transcript at page 14409. You noted that this entering the city is very tricky. And that's 14409 at page -- line 18 and 19. When you are saying that it was very tricky, you were thinking about how dangerous it is if you engage in fighting in a built-up area, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You should not forget, and I'm sorry I cannot answer only with yes, that I came up with the proposal that I described given the information that the OTP has given to me. If you describe me another scenario where -- where combat troops are located in Knin or in the direct environment of Knin, defending the city itself, so signs of road blocks, signs of trenches, then you get a different situation. But even then our first rule in the doctrine in urban environment is avoid battle in an urban environment. That's our first rule what we use.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, and I agree with you, and we will get into some of the reasons for that, but I hasten to add that there are troops in Knin which you mentioned. There are troops on the Dinara. If those troops for the ARSK are on the Dinara were withdrawing, where were they going to withdraw to? Were they going to go in a different direction, or were they going to do as General Mrksic said, Withdraw to our positions for the direct defence of Knin, as he mentioned in D106?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is it very logic, and I don't deny that. The point we are talking about is that the decisive defence can also be done in the complete environment outside the city, which the environment is extremely well for that because of the hillsides, because of the possibility that the defender has to build up trenches, to use his forces there. A defence does not necessarily mean a single line. A defence can be in the form of an area defence. So there are so many possibilities. And one of them is, of course, that you build up a defence inside the city and that you use everything single brick there to defend yourself. But I have to repeat myself, I have been given information by the OTP, and that is the analysis that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Colonel, I understand that you've been given just a limited amount of information, but given your expertise, I want to explore some of the ramifications of possible proposals accepting that possibly you didn't have information concerning other lines of resistance by the ARSK. If we are talking about dispensing with the artillery, and if we are talking about the withdraw of forces in defence of Knin, and if we are talking about the defence of Knin being a decisive defence down to the last man, we essentially are talking about an encirclement of Knin and the troops moving into Knin with the very strong possibility of fighting within the city limits of Knin, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you take -- if you start from the assumption that the combat troops -- that the ARSK combat troops are withdrawing into the city of Knin, then you end up in a very tricky situation. I admit that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's talk a little bit just because I want -- I certainly know what you're talking about, Colonel, but I'd like to use some of the literature we have to explore exactly what a tricky situation means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I'd like to call 1D65-0464.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 1D65-0464, Colonel, is a United States army infantrymen's guide to combat in built up areas. I understand this is -- it may in part be American doctrine. I have some additional information to show you concerning Dutch doctrine, so you can help us out about how you differ from anything that's in here. But basically when it comes to fighting in built up areas, FIBUA, I think they cal it, F-I-B-U-A, we're going to be talking about some of the broad strokes. And the first page I'd like to you about is page 7 of this document. Section 1-5, and just going to -- and just going with further explanation of your combat comment that it's tricky: "Built up areas consist mainly of man-made features such as buildings. Building provide cover and concealment, limited fields of observation and fire, and block movement of troops, especially mechanised troops. Thick-walled buildings provide ready-made fortified positions." During the course of your -- some your analysis, you noted that there are strong structures in Knin that can't be destroyed by artillery fire. These same strong structures likewise provide excellent cover for defending troops when they're fighting in built up areas, don't they?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll just show you the analogue to that which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like this. I'm going to refer to it again, but I would like to tender 1D65-0464.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How long is that document, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The document that I have uploaded is 15. I will be referring to the document again, Mr. President. There are other items in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1264.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit D1264 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'd like to call up 1D65-0282.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, is it true that the document we just admitted into evidence that we have no --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We only have an English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like the parties to spontaneously inform the Chamber if they are tendering documents. I mean, I'm now checking these things, but I think it would be appropriate if a party is aware of any shortcoming on what is regularly required for admission, that they draw the attention of the Chamber to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any problem as far as the other Defence teams or the Prosecution is concerned in relation to this infantryman's guide to combat. If not, then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider whether we would at any further moment insist on translation because apparently the parties in this courtroom have no problem with it. At the same time, the whole of the public on the documents is doing without, and the public character of this trial is important for this Chamber. We'll consider whether we'll ask for a translation to be provided. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just turning to a -- the next document on the screen, which is the combat operations. And going to paragraph 12094, Mr. President, there is not an English translation -- excuse me, a B/C/S translation of this document either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But it is it admitted into evidence already, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe it is a different section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, it's a different section.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Page 91. And if we could go 12094.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm interested in those first two sentences. This is I take it, you know, Dutch doctrine. "Depending on their size and location, built-up areas can represent key terrain. The obstacle value and the concealment and cover make built-up areas an ideal backbone for defensive operations." And that is basically what you were talking about previously, sir, that the defender has an advantage under these circumstances, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we hypothetically use street-to-street combat in Knin, we would be talking about the ARSK would have that advantage.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us turn back to D1264 and go into a couple of more aspects and go to section 1-8.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: By the way, Mr. President, I would offer into evidence the document that I just presented to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But only the page or the section you just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm going to refer to multiple sections in that document so ... there would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is 100-page document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do we have 100 pages, I believe?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least I've got 103. But ... which is -- which asks for a very selective approach --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will select those pages that I will use and just revamp the -- as opposed to putting 100 pages up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I know that I have seen this document before, but I do not know what portions exactly are in evidence and what portions are not. If you could upload the relevant sections and then an opportunity to Mr. Russo to consider whether he would like to add anything do it, and then a decision will be made on admission. But perhaps we could already reserve an exhibit number. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number D1265.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1265, which is a selection of relevant pages from the publication by the Royal Netherlands Army on combat operations, is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The other document that looked similar, Judge, is D1248.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But just staying with this 1-8 target engagement, it notes that: "Targets are usually briefly exposed at ranges of 100 metres or less. As a result, combat in built-up areas consists mostly of close, violent combat." Would you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us continue on to section 2-6 in the same manual. Several pages up, you will see, it is four pages up. And if we can just go one more page, to paragraph 12. On paragraph 12 talking about fighting in built-up areas: "Ammunition consumption is five to ten times greater in urban environments than in-field environments." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it is greater, whether it is it five to ten times, that is up to this publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we go back to D1265, the Royal Netherlands doctrine. 1265. And go to paragraph 937 [sic]. Talking about fighting in urbanised areas, 0937.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's it. Page 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Urbanised areas." Going to the second sentence. "These areas should be avoided if possible." Going down to the next paragraph. "The operation in built-up areas has a delaying effect on tempo." Staying with 938. This is -- going on to the next page: "Physically and mentally exhausting."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And going ahead to paragraph 11109.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll just tried, sir, and this is a lot of the same doctrine. "An attack in a built-up area usually gives rise to prolonged combat actions with heavy losses." So all those, sir, the defender having an advantage it being very violent, ammunition consumption high, it has a delaying tactic, being mentally and physically exhausting, and prolonged combat in fighting in built-up areas brings with it heavy losses. Do you agree with all the factors?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with all the factors, so that is the major reason to avoid in all cases to get drawn into an urban combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When we go into an urban combat area as a senior officer, sir, you know historically that fighting in built-up areas is also extremely harmful and detrimental to the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Because when we are fighting house to house in a town, history has told us that that fighting is taking place in civilian residences, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, likewise if we stay with Netherlands doctrine on this area and we go back to paragraph 0939, and I can -- 0939. That's good. Now when we're talking about 0939, talking about fighting in built-up areas, the infantry fighting in built-up areas supported by engineers and where possible by tanks, artillery, and air support. So according to Dutch doctrine where possible when you send your guys into fighting in a built-up area, you also want to soften up that terrain but using artillery when possible, don't they?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the very clear pronunciations when possible. And that when possible is dependent on main factors, especially on the close proximity of civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when -- just for the record, we are talking about the US army manual that notes that -- that section 3-5 in the document we have included, those types of offensive operations might require extensive air and artillery bombardment. And you would agree that when you're fighting in a built-up area, the use of artillery would be done trying to restrict an enemy's position in that area while also destroying his position. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Using artillery in any fight, including in an urban environment depends on the -- the effect that you want to achieve. That can be destruction, that can be -- there are no so many possibilities that you do that in support of the actions of your own forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What I'm trying to get at, sir, here is that when your going through fighting in a built-up area and are you fighting house to house against the enemy and an enemy using civilian structures, and you as the attacks Force Commander are moving through that area, you are going to be firing on what otherwise would be civilian structures simply because the enemy is housed in there, and you not dispense with the option of likewise using artillery in this entire endeavour. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you do an urban operation, you have all your weapon systems and all area military means available, and you can choose to use them or not to use them. That is up to the overall commander, and further on, to the commanders on the scene. That means the platoon commanders, the company commanders that do the actual fight. So they are able to send in a fire -- a request for a fire mission. That fire mission can be done by artillery, that can be done by mortars, that can be done by close air support. That's up to the commander on the scene to decide how to do that within his rules of engagement and within his possibilities, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, and when he is -- he is obviously history has shown us as you said when those decisions have been made historically, the entire operation of fighting in built-up areas, as you noted before, brings the possibility of significant -- of danger to the civilian population much higher, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because -- yes, in an urban environment there is an extremely high risk for the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you're fighting in a built-up area -- I mean, let's just go -- before we ask that question, let's just go to D1264, section 3-3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Page 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It says: "Due to the nature of combat in built-up areas, more troops are normally needed than in other combat situations." And that's because, Colonel, would you agree with that, firstly?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that's because when you're in continuous close combat, there is a tremendous amount of fatigue, psychological strain, and most importantly, casualties. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't heard anything new so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm just asking you --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right, you're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So if we look at what General Gotovina was faced, he was faced with the issue of the actual battle he conducted or faced the very possibility of, as Captain Dangerfield noted, a bloody last stand in fighting in an urban environment such as Knin, Which would have brought with it, a tremendous amend of casualties. Those are two very viable options that the General had to consider. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And a reasonable commander under those circumstances could quite validly pick the first option, i.e., artillery followed by the infantry assault as we saw in Operation Storm. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's one of the options, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, one of the issues that I'd just like to address you briefly and ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, just for me to understand, the two options you gave in your previous question, the one is that General Gotovina was faced with the issue of actual battle; or the very possibility of Captain Dangerfield's notion of a bloody last stand in fighting in an urban environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Or face the actual battle he conducted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where when it's not clear to me what the two options actually are. I don't know. Could you tell us how you understood the two options to be, when you answered the question, Mr. Konings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the last option I understand is -- is the defence until the last man --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The possibility.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The possibility of a defence until the last man, but in that option it is not clear to me whether that only concerns specifically the area -- the urban environment of Knin or the -- the whole environment, including the mountains around Knin, because that -- and the other possibility is that -- well, to be honest, I don't see the other option now as well so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it might be good that have you a clear understanding when asked if you answer a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can rephrase that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, of course if could you clarify the issue that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The other option that I was talking about, Colonel, is the option that was actually employed by General Gotovina in Operation Storm, those two options, conducting the operation as conducted in operation storm, or the other option of dispensing with artillery and moving solely with infantry with the possibility of engaging in a fight in an urban area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask Mr. Kehoe to be a bit for specific. The witness has clearly been given several versions, both from the Prosecution side and from the Defence as to what General Gotovina actually did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me, excuse me. [Overlapping speakers] ... if there is a speaking objection, I would ask that it be done outside of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends on what the objection is, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since Mr. Russo has not -- did not go into any further details, do I understand that the two options you are putting to this witness the one, the option of what Mr. Gotovina finally did. And the other option which I do not understand which did not take place was a street-to-street, man-to-man fight in the city of Knin. Now, even if you would not know in any way what Mr. Gotovina did, you could say, These are two options. The one what he did, and what he didn't do. But if we want to further explore these matters, then, of course, we would have to get into further details as what actually was done, because this witness has no personal observation, no personal knowledge of what happened and gathered his information partly from what he was told by the Prosecution, partly by what you told him, partly on the basis of documents. So if you want to pursue this matter, I think it would be good to know exactly what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, to be honest, the second option presented by counsel is not the option that I was trying to describe in my document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think it is it put to you by Mr. Kehoe. And he -- on the basis of some of the documents he had shown to him [sic], he apparently -- the Defence considers it is likely that that is what one could expect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is how I understood your final question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With these documents -- and as Judge Orie said, one without the attack employed during Operation Storm, one could expect that a fight in the -- urban environment would ensue. The course employed by General Gotovina as a reasonable commander -- as a military commander was a reasonable attempt to avoid that, avoid civilian casualties while likewise bringing about the demise of the army of the Republic of Serb Krajina. Isn't that a valid analysis of exactly what transpired with the two options that you have put forth in your report?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in itself, that sounds very likely, and I don't deny that the use of artillery against military targets, the high value military targets even when in a civilian environment. That is up to the commander that that is it a possibility. But it's still leaves me with the fact that artillery has been used for more than 24 hours, and it leaves me with the fact that I still do not have any explanation for the point that I was asked to address by the OTP, is the order that was given to shell the city of Knin. And there are many aspects in the operation described in -- in documents that are absolutely belonging to a military operation, and I don't deny that, and we have debating that. We have been talking about the use of troops, we have been talking about the use of artillery against military targets in conjunction with the military operation. We have extensively been debating about the risks of urban environment, competent urban environment. I tried to develop a scenario that -- based on the information given by the OTP where it says that there was inside Knin no defence, no coordinated defence, no combat forces, no nothing, only 4 to 500 individual soldiers that had no defence. I tried to develop an option that once the 4th or the 7th Brigade is broken through the Serb lines that that brigade could have moved quickly in an open formation to Knin, in order to take possession of Knin. Doing so they take risks. I understand that, but sometimes the commander has to lay the risk at his own forces in order to avoid civilian casualties. So, for me, there is still a disconnection between the order given, especially shelling the city of Knin and the way that was performed during the 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We will get to that order, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think if you want to take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break, and we will resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, I'd like to address with you now at this point, you know, some additional logic concerning the attack on Knin in the fashion that it was conducted by looking at the actual effect and -- and the -- while also looking at that damage that it did cause and the goals achieved. Obviously we talked before about Knin being the centre of gravity, but I'd like to go through a series of documents with you and just discuss them in the context of the success or failure of the operation, as you see it, in light of these documents. And first I'd like to talk to you about D389. Now, Colonel, D389 is an ARSK intelligence report from the ARSK General Staff accounting what happened on the morning of the 4th. And if we can go to the fourth paragraph down, it notes that: "Knin was attacked from Livanjsko Polje from several directions and by the time this information was drafted between 200 and 300 rounds of different calibers impacted on the town. The first strike was carried out on the building of the SVK General Staff ..." Now that is the location that we mentioned -- or you mentioned, Colonel, is the most significant strategic target for the ARSK in Knin. Correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And frankly the most significant strategic target for the ARSK throughout the Krajina, right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This said: "... which suffered great ... damage with the fleet of vehicles almost completely destroyed. Later the fire was transferred on the military barracks 1300 Kaplara, the Tvik factory, the railway intersection, residential buildings in the area beneath the Knin fortress," et cetera? If we could turn our attention to 65 ter 1006. This is an intelligence report by the HV for the 6th of August after Storm. Just dealing with the first page of this: "The enemy communication system has been completely disabled and there by the command system on almost all levels which increased the level of chaos in the remaining units of the routed army of the Serb Krajina in the Republic of Croatia except ... 11th eastern Slavonia corps." Now, when you were going through the purposes of artillery and you wanted to create a degree of confusion and suppression, this would appear to be a successful conclusion at least in part of the artillery operation, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this entry here suggests that the disabling of the communication system was done by artillery, then your conclusion is correct. But that doesn't state it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll like to offer into evidence 65 ter 1006.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1266, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And one last report on this score, which is 65 ter 1666.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is an intelligence report by the HV of 5 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can turn to the second page in the English, and I believe it is the -- if I may, still the first page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And it notes about the successes -- at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can we just scroll that up a just little bit to the top of the page. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Two SVK corps were completely broken up, 7th Knin and 15th Lika corps. Now, are you familiar with the lotion of the ARSK 15th Lika corps?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will tell you that evidence is that the 15th Lika corps was in the Gospic Military District which was to the north of the Split Military District. Now, this reflects that both of these corps were destroyed. To the --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say that, it says broken up. It is not the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Broken up?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is quite a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We'll just stay with the terminology there. "The state and military structure was completely deprived of its leadership by the liberation of Knin which had a significant effect on the collapse of the morale of the civilian population and military units ..." Moving down the page, just to the -- if you can scroll down: "The single system of commanding has been broken up including the communications system so that the SVK is no longer functioning." Now you know from the documents that you reviewed that the HV's artillery directed its fire on the communication system of the ARSK. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And from this document, you can conclude that that ARSK communications system was destroyed and that these two Corps defending the ARSK were broken up?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, the document does not talk about -- specifically about artillery. It talks about, in generic, about the results that were contain, and I assume that the use of artillery was a part of that, but that indeed the whole Operation Storm achieved this -- the goal or the end is that is described here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you one last document on this score, D819 which is a sitrep or a message, I take that back, from UNCRO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: By the way, Your Honour, we'll offer 65 ter 1666 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1267.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you can just look at this front sheet. I'm not saying -- you may not be familiar with this document, Colonel, but you are familiar with these types of messages going from UNCRO, the formatting in any event?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know these messages. I have been writing them myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in the message they deal with what happened with the ARSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can turn over to the next page. Scroll that down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "The rapid collapse of ARSK after the initial breakthrough can be explained as follow [sic]: "Poor leadership at intermediate levels has been observed. Absence of a counterattack reserve armour has been observed in only one echelon." Paragraph 4-3: "Total lack of theatre 3CI capacities and leaders were not trained for coordinated theatre level OPs." Now when they say, "total lack of 3CI capacities," what is that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that there is in old theatre no command and control and communications and information capacity is available. That is a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So from this assessment made by UNCRO on the 7th of August, in part, the collapse of the ARSK came down to a lack of command, control, communications, and intelligence capacities.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only, there is much more. The assessment of the UNCRO says much more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. I'm just in that paragraph, sir.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which paragraph are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That paragraph says it says more than only C3 capacities, and it says leaders were not trained for coordinated theatre level OPs. That is not something that is in place already quite long. What I want to say, you focus on point 43, that's fine. But when he read through this, then this is an extensive array of possible reasons, only possible reasons that the breakthrough was explained by, and that is much more than only the follow-up of one Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, sir.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But would you agree with me that if an entity's command, control, communications, and intelligence abilities are destroyed or significantly damaged, that will give to the attacking force a significant benefit?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, I know that you have been shown P64 which was the intelligence assessment -- excuse me, the damage assessment by Lieutenant-Colonel Hjertnes. Were you shown any other reports on that score about -- for instance, the CIVPOL report?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first try to recollect the report that you -- the P64 that you are referring.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that is the UNMO report from the city in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me bring that up on the screen, P64.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Tab 23 in the witness's binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is the document that I'm talking about on the screen, that in paragraph 2 that the: "In general, shelling was concentrated against military objectives. The damage [sic] caused by shelling to civilian establishments is concentrated to the close vicinity of military objectives. Only three to five impacts is observed in other urban areas."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's will turn to P228, which is a CIVPOL assessment, UNCIVPOL.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again an assessment of 18th of August 1995. He notes -- a survey of a Knin town to assess the damage done in Knin town caused by shelling, arson, and wilful damage. "We covered the whole township and observed several impacts of shells and rockets around the Tvik factory. Milicija headquarters, general of the northern barracks ... government house, Knin radio, TV, and the hillside below Knin ... We found roughly -- excuse me. The compound of the northern barracks was not checked. Observations done from the street [sic]. "We counted roughly 20 houses, buildings hit by shells and ... another 20 presumable damaged by arson." Now with the items that are set forth in paragraph 2, those are, in fact, the targets that we reviewed before and that you described as, in some instances military targets, right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. And without being exact, the assessment by UNCIVPOL seems to be in line with what the UNMO, Lieutenant-Colonel Hjertnes said was the damage in P64?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Russo. The objection would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That -- the fact that this is consistent in terms of the damage with P64.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is the objection that it misrepresents -- could you then go into further details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He can say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I mean, the answer is --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: He is not asking him if it is consistent. He is putting to him that it is it consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's a question. It's cross-examination. The question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please point exactly to the language where you say that the assessment is the same, so that where Mr. Russo apparently may have some problems, that we know exactly what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, would you agree that the damage as reflected in P64 from shelling is consistent, not exactly the same but consistent with the analysis of the damage done by UNCIVPOL in P228.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is it consistent with respect to the level of damage that is -- that is it reported, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to D66. This is a United States government cable after a visit to Knin, and I believe the evidence is that it was on the 7th of August. The cable is dated the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we go to the bottom of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Downtown Knin. Although Knin was reportedly heavily shelled in the early hours of the hostilities, few downtown buildings and residential areas showed signs of shell damage." Now, had you seen this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you put these documents together, sir, can you not conclude or do you conclude, number 1, that the shelling by the HV on the 4th and the 5th was directed towards military targets, or military objectives; let me say that.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, insofar as you go along with the UNMO document, but the UNMO document is not completed. That's stated at the end. It is only a preliminary investigation which was done to an -- apparently a certain area of the city, and focussing on that document, it says indeed that most of the shelling was done on military targets, we have had our discussion about military targets, and that there was caused damage to the civilian property close to the military targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me help you out that Colonel Hjertnes gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in January of this year. In paragraph 33 of that statement, where he noted that his final report was consistent with the provisional assessment, and an UN public informations officer, Alun Roberts, previously advised this Chamber in a trial transcript 7079, line 19, through 7081, line 8, that the final assessment that was conducted was consistent with the provisional assessment. So the evidence that's before the Chamber is that that provisional assessment was consistent with the [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going object to the last portion of Mr. Kehoe's question. Without going into the additional evidence, the information he put to him may suggest that but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say this evidence before the Chamber is not necessarily the evidence that's before the Chamber, because there may be more evidence, so Mr. Kehoe that's -- and would you also have the exhibit number for me the statement, paragraph 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It has been read into evidence during the course of Alun Roberts's testimony. He has not testified yet, so it has not been offered into evidence yet. I'm talking about -- that's Colonel Hjertnes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just see. One second. The statement of Hjertnes is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: January 15, 17th. Paragraph 33, January --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, because as far as making it as an exhibit when the witness has not testified yet with something that could be -- the Chamber gave some guidance on that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I remember the problem. Therefore that is not in evidence at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have a 1D number on, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but no, it's just ... so the evidence that is before the Chamber, you said in the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That, in fact, was used during the course of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I'll check -- that's on you said 7079.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Through page 7081, line 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's go back to where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the e-court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we've ruled the objection. So that is in the evidence that is before this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you put the question again to the witness in order not to -- he may have forgotten what it really was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. President, the Steinar Hjertnes' statement that is in e-court is 1D10 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have no access to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Apologies. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If can I just go back and read that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, my question, and we just go back through this, Colonel, is that -- and I think you answered this in the sense of the evidence that was set forth in both the provisional assessment that we now know is a final assessment, was not the same but consistent with what happened -- the evidence in CIVPOL and likewise was consistent with the report by the United States monitors in the 7th of August that few downtown buildings and residential areas showed signs of shell damage.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I have said that. I said that the consistency is lying in the level of damage because the UNMO uses the word military targets. The CIVPOL report does not use that as far as I recollect, nor does the report -- the report of the US representative. So there are some differences in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Turning our attention to the -- if we can go back to the provisional assessment, P64. And looking at the paragraph 2, were you shown any documents by the OTP that indicated that the shelling was more widespread than that as described by Colonel Hjertnes in paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So would you agree with me that in looking at what actually transpired in this shelling endeavour that the centre of gravity Knin was taken out for the entire Krajina, not just in Sector South, that they didn't engage in something akin to fighting in built-up areas, and that very quickly the communications for the ARSK was so damaged that it ultimately led to the deadline and fall of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask that it broken up. It's compound in several ways. I'm just going to ask that that be broken up into individual questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If the witness can look at and disagree or nuance any version, any form of it that he so desires.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me re-read the question. Before you answer that question, Mr. Konings, I would invite you to carefully read the question which is a composite question on the screen in front of you and to see whether you, in its entirety, you would agree with everything Mr. Kehoe put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I have the idea that this is -- this conclusion of Mr. Kehoe is now directly connected to this -- this sole UNMO report. And reading his conclusion, if that is true what I'm saying, that is going, to me, way too far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the answer is simply no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if you want to know more, Mr. Kehoe, then splitting up the question might assist you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You would agree that the artillery attack -- you would agree the artillery attack successfully brought down the centre of gravity for the Republic of the Serb Krajina. You would agree with that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you agree that this centre of gravity was a location that was important, essential not only for Knin but for the entire Krajina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to go back to your previous question where I said yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That possible Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because to bring it in splendid isolation that the artillery attack successfully brought down the centre of gravity, I don't think that is a pure yes. If you talk about that, then the artillery attack has a role in that, and I don't deny that can be a large role, but I do think that we have way we have described Operation Storm that the complete operation is -- is the basis for the total breakdown of the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you for that additional explanation. And as a result of the actions taken in Operation Storm, Knin both on the ARSK side and the HV side, was not forced to fight in a built-up area taking on significant casualties on both sides as well as the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the speed with which Operation Storm compromised the communications facilities of the ARSK in Knin led to a significant damage to the combat capabilities of the ARSK. Again, not only in Sector South but throughout the Krajina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would you conclude, based on this, Colonel, that this was a very successful operation by the HV?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the military part is concerning [sic], yes. But I still have one burning question left before I say -- before I give you any answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, with regard to -- we talked about this previously, and have you no knowledge as to any collateral damage to the civilian population, do you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not my burning question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. That is my question.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no -- I have no information about collateral damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's talk to the issue that you raised concerning the order itself, and I trust your burning questions comes from your disagreement with the phraseology employed in the combat order, P1125.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So let's turn to that. And if we can turn to the next page. Actually, two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I want to give you the front page, Colonel, just so you see it. Now this is the order with which you take issue. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Russo, is this a tab in the Colonel's book? If I may, it may be easier to deal with it in paper. If it is not, we can just deal with the screen but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, it's, tab 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, colonel, just paging through this order, I mean, it -- just going through it, the first page, I mean, there is extensive information on the status of the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can we turn to page 2. Can we go to the next page in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And it gives very -- it gives tasks at the bottom of the page to the entities of the Split Military District. "The Split Military District shall prepare and carry out joint offensive operation in the following [sic] areas." And gives the areas, northern Dalmatia, western Bosnia, Kupres with the following task, and he tells them what to do. This is General Gotovina. "A vigorous attack with intense artillery and air support on direct axes directed at main military and political transportation features in the enemy's operational depth, break up the enemy on the forward defence line, and decisively advance and take control of the key land transportation military and political features, thus putting the enemy in a no-exit situation and forcing him to surrender or withdraw." Now, Colonel, that's a very specific task that General Gotovina is giving to his -- or the soldiers in the Split Military District, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this individual task that he is ordering is not only going out to the infantry. It's an order that is going to artillery units as well. Right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So he is telling them what he wants them to do.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Then he notes: "What he has decided to do." And have you read -- going through paragraph 4 --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the detail with which he phases this operation?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Then he gives very specific detail in paragraph 5 as --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... 6, excuse me, paragraph 5 on page 6, 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page. Page 8. Page 9. Next page. Next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page 10 is task for Operative Group Sibenik. Page -- two pages up is Operation Group Zadar. As is page 13. Now, he is telling them the particular areas that he wants them to move on, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all respect, sir, this is up so far in what you are saying, I have nothing to disagree with because it is a regular normal military order which in NATO we would have worded in another way, but it is an order that specifies the tasks for the underlying brigades of the various operational groups. I have no problem with that wording or with the specification of the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let stay with that, Colonel. And let's look at a portion -- another portion of a document that we received -- part of it we received in evidence. We didn't receive this portion, but it is 1D65-0481. Can you recognise this document, do you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what we're dealing with is just chapter 6 or a portion of chapter 6 on plans and orders, and I would like to direct your attention to 0654, which is the next page. "0564, an operation order should include only such detail as is necessary for commanders of subordinate formations or units to act purposefully, to issue their own orders and to ensure coordination. Mission command requires orders that concentrate on imparting an understanding of the context of the operation and what needs to be done rather than how it is to be achieved." Now you recognise that, that is what an operational commander will do? He will tell his subordinates, as General Gotovina does in this document, what, in fact, should be taken but leaves it to the individuals exactly how they are going to -- their infantry, for instance, is going to operate?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certain -- in many cases he will -- mission command means that underlying or lower commanders are allowed to fill in the -- to use their own initiative in order to meet the commander's intent. But there are also other things that have to be arranged very carefully ahead and that are not directly falling under the aspect of mission command. So everything that's concerning rules of engagement, that kind of information, might be specified up to the fucking detail, I'm sorry that I used that word, in annexes of operational orders, in target lists, et cetera. So on the one hand, you are absolutely right. That is the purpose of mission command, and on the other hand, also with mission command, you have to arrange a lot of aspects in detail and write them down so that everybody knows exactly what the commander means in that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I mean, let's look at -- let's turn our attention to the area. I mean -- by the way if we can tender this into evidence Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is Exhibit D1268, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit D1268 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Kehoe, I'm looking at the clock. I don't know whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It might take a while to go through this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
